config.title: Design Auth Flow

intro.title: Design Auth Flow
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple authentication flow for an Angular application, allowing users to log in and log out. You will learn how to manage user state using Angular services and handle authentication logic. The main technologies involved are Angular services for state management, TypeScript for type safety, and Angular templates for the user interface. By the end, you will understand how to structure a basic auth system to control access in your apps.
intro.usecase: Authentication flows are a foundational security pattern in nearly every modern web application, from e-commerce sites like Amazon to productivity tools like Google Workspace. As a developer, you'll implement these flows to manage user login, registration, and session handling in dashboards, admin panels, and customer portals. This lesson teaches you to design a structured, maintainable auth flow in Angular, a critical skill for building secure, professional applications that protect user data and control access to features.

objectives: Construct an Angular component to serve as the main authentication interface
Configure routing to navigate between login and registration views
Initialize reactive forms for user input in authentication components
Implement form validation to control user data submission
Bind form controls to component properties for data manipulation
Integrate authentication services with UI components
Render conditional UI elements based on authentication state

steps.title: Import Angular modules and components for auth flow
steps.instruction: Import Component and OnInit from '@angular/core' and FormsModule from '@angular/forms' at the top of your TypeScript file.
steps.hint: Use the import keyword followed by the symbols you need from their respective Angular packages.
steps.seedCode:
// Import Angular modules and components here

// Your component will go below
steps.expectedOutcome: The necessary Angular modules for building authentication components are imported.
successCriteria: Component and OnInit are imported from '@angular/core', and FormsModule is imported from '@angular/forms'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've imported some modules, but check if you have all three: Component and OnInit from '@angular/core', and FormsModule from '@angular/forms'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The imports are missing or incorrect. Make sure to import Component and OnInit from '@angular/core', and FormsModule from '@angular/forms' using the import syntax.

steps.title: Create the main AuthFlowComponent
steps.instruction: Create the AuthFlowComponent class with the @Component decorator and implement the OnInit interface.
steps.hint: Define a class named AuthFlowComponent, add the @Component decorator above it, and use 'implements OnInit' after the class name.
steps.expectedOutcome: The AuthFlowComponent class is defined with the @Component decorator and implements OnInit.
successCriteria: AuthFlowComponent class exists, has @Component decorator with selector and template, and implements OnInit interface.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your class has the @Component decorator and implements OnInit.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you defined a class named AuthFlowComponent with @Component and implements OnInit.

steps.title: Initialize authentication state variables
steps.instruction: Inside the AuthFlowComponent class, declare two properties: isLoggedIn (boolean) and userEmail (string). Initialize isLoggedIn to false and userEmail to an empty string.
steps.hint: Add these properties directly in the class body, using TypeScript type annotations. For example: isLoggedIn: boolean = false;
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have two typed properties to track authentication status and user email.
successCriteria: AuthFlowComponent has isLoggedIn (boolean, initialized to false) and userEmail (string, initialized to '') as class properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've declared the properties, but check that isLoggedIn is boolean (initialized to false) and userEmail is string (initialized to '').
steps.feedbackWrong: The properties are missing or incorrectly typed. Declare isLoggedIn: boolean = false; and userEmail: string = ''; inside the class.

steps.title: Define login form data model
steps.instruction: Inside the AuthFlowComponent class, create a TypeScript interface named LoginForm with email and password properties. Both should be strings.
steps.hint: Define the interface above the class or inside the component file. Use the 'interface' keyword followed by property declarations with type annotations.
steps.expectedOutcome: The LoginForm interface is defined with email and password properties, both typed as strings.
successCriteria: LoginForm interface exists with email: string and password: string properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure both email and password properties are defined with string types.
steps.feedbackWrong: The interface definition is missing or incorrect. Remember to use the 'interface' keyword with proper TypeScript syntax.

steps.title: Initialize login form data object
steps.instruction: In the AuthFlowComponent class, create a property called 'loginForm' of type 'LoginForm' and initialize it with empty values for email and password.
steps.hint: You can create the property right after the existing state variables. Use the LoginForm interface you defined earlier.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now has a loginForm property properly typed and initialized with empty email and password fields.
successCriteria: The AuthFlowComponent has a loginForm property of type LoginForm initialized with empty string values for email and password.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure the loginForm property is typed as 'LoginForm' and initialized with both email and password fields set to empty strings.
steps.feedbackWrong: The loginForm property wasn't properly initialized. Check that you've created a property with the correct type and initialized it with empty email and password values.

steps.title: Create login handler method
steps.instruction: Inside the AuthFlowComponent class, define a method named onLogin() that sets isLoggedIn to true and userEmail to the email from loginForm.
steps.hint: Remember to use 'this' keyword to access component properties and methods.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now has a method that will handle login logic by updating authentication state.
successCriteria: The AuthFlowComponent has an onLogin() method that sets isLoggedIn to true and userEmail to loginForm.email.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created the onLogin method, but it needs to properly update both isLoggedIn and userEmail properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: The onLogin method is missing or doesn't update the authentication state correctly.

steps.title: Create logout handler method
steps.instruction: In your AuthFlowComponent class, define a method named onLogout that sets isLoggedIn to false and clears userEmail.
steps.hint: Add a method inside the class that updates the component's state properties.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a logout handler that resets authentication state.
successCriteria: The onLogout method is defined, sets isLoggedIn to false, and sets userEmail to an empty string.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've defined the onLogout method, but make sure it sets both isLoggedIn to false and userEmail to an empty string.
steps.feedbackWrong: The logout handler is not properly defined. Check that you've added the onLogout method inside the component class with the correct state updates.

steps.title: Set up component template structure
steps.instruction: Add a main container div with the class 'auth-container' to the component's template.
steps.hint: Inside the template property of the @Component decorator, add a <div> element with class='auth-container'.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component template now has a main container div that will hold the auth flow content.
successCriteria: The template property contains a <div> element with class='auth-container'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've added a <div> with exactly class='auth-container' inside the template property.
steps.feedbackWrong: The template should contain a <div> element with class='auth-container'. Check that you've added it correctly.

steps.title: Implement login form with two-way binding
steps.instruction: In the component's template, add an email input field with [(ngModel)] binding to loginForm.email and a password input field with [(ngModel)] binding to loginForm.password.
steps.hint: Use the ngModel directive with two-way binding syntax [(ngModel)] to connect the input fields to your loginForm object properties.
steps.analogousExample:
<!-- Example: binding an input to a component property -->
<input type="text" [(ngModel)]="userName" />
steps.expectedOutcome: The template will have two input fields (email and password) that are bound to the loginForm object properties using Angular's two-way data binding.
successCriteria: Email input field has [(ngModel)]="loginForm.email" and password input field has [(ngModel)]="loginForm.password" in the template.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some form fields, but make sure both email and password inputs have the [(ngModel)] binding syntax with the correct property names (loginForm.email and loginForm.password).
steps.feedbackWrong: The template doesn't contain the required two-way binding for both email and password fields. Remember to use [(ngModel)] syntax to bind to loginForm.email and loginForm.password.

steps.title: Add login button and wire click event
steps.instruction: In the component's template, add a button element with the text 'Login' and bind its click event to the onLogin method using Angular's event binding syntax.
steps.hint: Use the (click) event binding to call the onLogin method when the button is clicked.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: Button with click event binding
<button (click)="handleClick()">Click me</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A button with the label 'Login' appears in the component's template, and clicking it triggers the onLogin method.
successCriteria: The template contains a button element with text 'Login' and (click)="onLogin()" event binding.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you have a button with the text 'Login' and the (click)="onLogin()" event binding in the template.
steps.feedbackWrong: The login button with click event binding is missing. Add a button element with (click)="onLogin()" and text 'Login' to the template.
